# PsyStat: A calculator for the book "Psychological Statistics: The Basics"
# Developed by Tom Faulkenberry and Keelyn Brennan
# version: October 27, 2025
# updates to analytic Bayes factor calculations from ANOVA summaries

# libraries
library(shiny)

# make navbar pages
fluidPage(
  shinyUI(navbarPage("PsyStat", 
                     tabPanel("Probability calculator",
                              source("prob.R")$value
                              ),

                     tabPanel("Bayes factor calculator",
                              source("bayes.R")$value
                              ),
                    
                     tabPanel("About",
                              source("about_page.R")$value
                              )
                     )
  )
)

name: about_page.R
content:
fluidPage( HTML(r"(

About PsyStat

PsyStat was designed by Tom Faulkenberry (with help from Keelyn Brennan) to accompany the book Psychological Statistics: The Basics, published in 2022 by Routledge.


If you use this calculator in your scholarly work, we would appreciate it if you would cite it using the book's reference:

  • Faulkenberry, T. J. (2022). Psychological Statistics: The Basics. New York: Routledge.

In particular, this calculator is the only tool we know of for calculating Bayes factors directly from summary statistics in ANOVA designs. If you use PsyStat for this purpose, please consult (and cite!) the following papers:

  • Faulkenberry, T. J. (2021). The Pearson Bayes factor: An analytic formula for computing evidential value from minimal summary statistics. Biometrical Letters, 58(1), 1-26. https://doi.org/10.2478/bile-2021-0001
  • Faulkenberry, T. J., & Brennan, K. B. (2023). Computing analytic Bayes factors from summary statistics in repeated-measures designs. Biometrical Letters, 60(1), 1-21. https://doi.org/10.2478/bile-2023-0001

Note: many design elements of PsyStat are adapted from previous work by Erin Buchanan and Mine Cetinkaya-Rundel.


For complete source code, visit my Github page.

)") )

name: add_social_meta.py
content:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Re-apply social-preview (Open Graph / Twitter Card) meta tags to a
shinylive::export()'d index.html.

Run this once after every future `shinylive::export()`, since a fresh
export always regenerates a bare index.html with <title>Shiny App</title>
and no description/OG tags -- which is what made LinkedIn/Twitter/Facebook
show an ugly, title-less link preview.

Usage:
    python3 add_social_meta.py /path/to/exported/psystat/index.html
"""
import sys

TITLE = "PsyStat"
DESCRIPTION = (
    "A free, browser-based calculator for probabilities and Bayes factors "
    "(t-tests, correlations, ANOVA) -- companion app to "
    "Psychological Statistics: The Basics."
)
URL = "https://tomfaulkenberry.github.io/psystat/"

META_BLOCK = f"""    <title>{TITLE}</title>
    <meta name="description" content="{DESCRIPTION}" />

    <meta property="og:type" content="website" />
    <meta property="og:url" content="{URL}" />
    <meta property="og:title" content="{TITLE}" />
    <meta property="og:description" content="{DESCRIPTION}" />

    <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary" />
    <meta name="twitter:title" content="{TITLE}" />
    <meta name="twitter:description" content="{DESCRIPTION}" />"""


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        print(__doc__)
        sys.exit(1)

    path = sys.argv[1]
    with open(path) as f:
        content = f.read()

    if f"<title>{TITLE}</title>" in content:
        print("Already patched -- nothing to do.")
        return

    old_title = "    <title>Shiny App</title>"
    if old_title not in content:
        print(
            "Could not find the default '<title>Shiny App</title>' line. "
            "The shinylive export format may have changed -- edit this "
            "script's OLD_TITLE / logic, or patch index.html by hand."
        )
        sys.exit(1)

    content = content.replace(old_title, META_BLOCK)
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        f.write(content)
    print(f"Patched {path}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

name: bayes.R
content:
fluidRow( # input goes here column(4, ##change the title here div(helpText('Bayes factor calculator'), align = "left", style="font-size:140%"), br(), radioButtons(inputId = "test", label = "Test:", choiceNames = c("t-test", "correlation", "ANOVA"), choiceValues = c("ttest", "cor", "anova"), selected = "ttest" ), radioButtons(inputId = "design", label = "Design:", choiceNames = c("Single sample", "Independent samples"), choiceValues = c("single", "independent"), selected = "single" ), radioButtons(inputId = "direction", label = "Predicted direction:", choiceNames = c("None", "Positive effect", "Negative effect"), choiceValues = c("none", "positive", "negative"), selected = "none" ), uiOutput("statistic"), uiOutput("sample1"), uiOutput("sample2"), numericInput(inputId = "pH0", label = "Prior probability of null:", value=0.5, min=0, max=1, step=0.1 ) #submitButton("Calculate") ), # close column 1 # output goes here column(8, tabsetPanel( tabPanel("Summary", div(helpText('Model definitions:'), align = "left", style="font-size:140%"), div(uiOutput("nullText"), style="font-size:130%"), div(uiOutput("altText"), style="font-size:130%"), br(), div(helpText('Predictive adequacy:'), align = "left", style="font-size:140%"), plotOutput("pizza"), div(helpText('Bayes factors:'), style="font-size:140%"), div(uiOutput("bfText"), align = "left", style="font-size:130%;"), div(uiOutput("description"), align = "left", style="font-size:130%"), br(), div(helpText('Posterior probabilities:'), style="font-size:140%"), div(uiOutput("postNull"), align = "left", style="font-size:130%;"), div(uiOutput("postAlt"), align = "left", style="font-size:130%") ), tabPanel("Help", HTML(r"(

What this calculator does

This tool computes a Bayes factor -- a measure of the strength of evidence in your data for one hypothesis over another -- for three common designs: a t-test (one-sample or independent samples), a Pearson correlation, and a one-way ANOVA (between-subjects or repeated-measures). It works directly from the summary statistics you'd normally report in a paper (a t-statistic, an observed correlation, or an F-statistic with its degrees of freedom) rather than requiring your raw data.

How to use it

  1. Choose the Test (t-test, correlation, or ANOVA) and, for t-tests, the Design (single sample or independent samples) and any Predicted direction for a one-sided test.
  2. Enter the test statistic reported by your analysis (t, observed correlation r, or F) along with the relevant sample size(s) or degrees of freedom.
  3. Set the Prior probability of null -- how likely you believed the null hypothesis was before seeing the data (0.5 is a neutral default).
  4. Read the results in the Summary panel: the null and alternative hypotheses being compared, the "pizza plot" showing the relative predictive adequacy of each, the Bayes factor itself (BF10 and BF01), and the resulting posterior probabilities.

A Bayes factor of, say, BF10 = 5 means the observed data are 5 times more likely under the alternative hypothesis than under the null -- evidence favoring the alternative. A value less than 1 (equivalently, BF01 greater than 1) favors the null instead.

For a walkthrough, watch: PsyStat Bayes factor calculator (YouTube).

)") ) ) ) # close column ) # close fluid row

What this calculator does

This tool finds the probability (area under the curve) associated with a region of the Normal, t, or F distribution -- the same calculation behind a p-value or a critical-value table, done interactively with a plot.

How to use it

  1. Choose a Distribution (Normal, t, or F) and enter its parameters (mean and standard deviation for Normal; degrees of freedom for t and F).
  2. Choose which Region you want the area for: a lower tail, an upper tail, both tails, or the middle.
  3. Enter the boundary value(s), a (and b, if the region needs two boundaries).
  4. The plot shades the requested region, and the probability is reported below it as p = ...

For a walkthrough, watch: PsyStat probability calculator (YouTube).
